blocks.p: It was past one in the morning when Rei came out of Jūjō station. The shopping street by the station had pulled down its shutters, and only the konbini on the corner was still lit, its doors sighing open for a man buying cigarettes. Rei walked the short way home past the shrine. Its wooden gate was dark, and a single Obon lantern hung by the offering box, burning low. Behind the shrine, the windows of the flat were black. On the floor of the genkan lay a sheet of folded paper that someone had pushed under the door. Rei picked it up, put it on the table without opening it, and went to fetch the rest.
He took everything back to the kitchen. The kitchen was where all this had begun. That month he had learned that he understood a thing best in the room where it had cost him the most.

He laid the bookseller's ledger, Gin's book and his own rough copies across the table where the kettle had gone cold on the first morning. Then he made himself write the whole machine out as one sentence. That was how his father had taught him to find the lie in a set of accounts. "If you cannot say it in a sentence," his father used to say, "you do not yet know what you are looking at." Rei had been looking at this for a month without saying it.
So he wrote it.

A chair emptied in 2009 has leaned on Kita-ku for six years, and a patient demon wearing my brother is helping the wall finish a fall the empty chair began, so that on the last night of Obon something can step into the open thirteenth office and call the wall's collapse a mending.
One sentence. He read it three times. It did not get any less true.

He turned to the back of Gin's book, to the map Gin had drawn of the ward. The sentence had a direction in it, and he wanted to see that direction on paper. The map was there, in Gin's small, exact printing. The flat behind Jūjō Shrine. The station four hundred metres to the southwest. And a pencilled circle about three hundred metres to the northeast of the flat, with no label at all, only a note in the margin. Warmer here. I chose the flat by it without knowing what I was choosing. The wall did not lean north by accident. It leaned toward whatever Gin had felt in that circle, and toward the seat that had stood empty in Kita since the year the lights went grey.
Under the sentence he wrote three words, one under the other. Then he sat looking at them while the kettle ticked as it cooled. Fall. Gin. Me.
He had spent four weeks hoping the fog was hiding a fourth word. It was not. He made himself look at each word long enough to see where it led.

Behind the first word, the seat stayed empty and the seam finished tearing. He could see it with horrible ease, because he had walked the ward all month. The lanterns would never stop coming down the river. Watanabe would go grey at the edges and then go out, at the returns cart in Itabashi, between one book and the next. After him the others would go, one seat at a time. Obon would simply never end. The dead would keep coming home to a district that could no longer tell them apart from the living.

Behind the second word was Gin. Gin's worn body, already shaped to fit, already most of the way into the chair the Healer had walked it toward. The wall would mend. The twelve would stop being crushed. And Rei would carry home a grey cardigan two sizes too big and hang it on the hook beside the empty one for keys. He would visit something in the north of the city that had his brother's face and no brother in it.

Behind the third word was himself. Two pressed-down registers. A hand already printed with the grain of the wound, the one living person the far shore had made fit by accident when it sent him in to touch the tear. He could only picture it one way, and that way was Watanabe. A weather with a person left over. Holding up the north of the city every morning by agreeing to be crushed, until he weakened, and some stranger with a borrowed newspaper sat in a library to watch him put books back on the shelves.
He put the pen down. His hand was shaking, and that annoyed him, as if the hand belonged to someone else.

There was a fourth word after all, and it was not his. It was in the sheet of paper from the genkan floor. It had been pushed under the door some time in the evening, while he was in Shin-Ōkubo. It was a single sheet folded twice, in handwriting he knew from the small white room at Ōji.

doc.title: Folded note, unsigned, in Okada Shizuka's hand
lines: Rei. I am not supposed to know this and you are not supposed to have it.

The Office of Public Confidence has a draft on the Minister's desk. Hagiwara Mizuki calls it the Closing. Catalogue every medium in the city. Contain them. Then force the veil shut by sealing the axis at the centre of it. Permanently.

It would trap the good, the evil and everyone in between on the wrong side, forever. The dead who want to come home. The ones who should never come back. Whatever is left of anyone who is in between. She knows that. She thinks it is the kind price.
Kita is her proof that the veil cannot be managed. She will use whatever happens on the last night as the reason.
Adachi cannot stand her and cannot move against her. Several of the Tower houses back her. He is the only door to the President, if anyone can move him.

blocks.p: Rei did not burn it. He laid it flat beside Gin's book. Then he opened the book to the chapter Gin had put off writing the longest, the one about who controlled what.

blocks.cap: Director Adachi Kenshin of the CVD

doc.title: Gin's book, Chapter Twenty-Three. The Political World
lines: A Tuesday. Rain again. I put this one off the longest, because politics keeps better in the dark, and so, lately, do I.

The CVD operates under the Ministry of Internal Affairs as a registered public agency. The Ministry provides budget, legal authority and political cover. The CVD provides expertise the Ministry cannot replicate and results the Ministry can present publicly. Neither discusses this explicitly. It is the kind of relationship that functions until it doesn't.
Three positions exist on veil policy.
Full Integration. Veil-aware governance. Practitioners get legal personhood protections. The CVD expands its public mandate and cuts classified operations.

Current Management. Keep the 1962 Accord. The present balance between public acknowledgment and classified management is the correct one. Registered practitioners stay in the asset development pipeline. The Grid stays in a legal grey area.

Suppression. The veil should be denied, contained and weaponised quietly. 'Practitioners are assets of the state, not citizens with rights.' It would absorb the CVD into intelligence and end the Grid. It has been losing ground since 1985 but keeps influence in specific ministry offices.

Director Adachi built the Division from an intelligence apparatus into something closer to its stated mandate. This is real. The asset development pipeline still exists. Both things are true and the tension does not resolve.

The political map the Division circulates puts the families in one colour, the Grid in another, and the CVD in the centre, larger than both. Every map is drawn by someone, and the someone is always in the middle of it. I keep my own version. The middle of mine is left empty on purpose.

blocks.p: Rei had to read the page twice before it came clear, so he put it into plain words for himself. The CVD was not free. It answered to a government ministry, which gave it money and legal cover in return for results. And in the offices above it, people argued about what to do with the veil. Some wanted to bring it into the open and give practitioners rights. Some wanted to keep things as they were under the old Accord of 1962. And some wanted the opposite, to deny the veil, lock it down and treat every practitioner as a tool owned by the state.

He read the line about the map three times, the way he had read his own sentence. The middle of mine is left empty on purpose. Gin had drawn the city with a hole where the power should be. Hagiwara Mizuki wanted to fill that hole with a lid.

blocks.cap: The political world above the CVD

blocks.p: He understood her better than he wanted to. She sat in a glass office in Marunouchi, above the CVD's public face, and she was the third position on Gin's page, given a budget and a kind voice. It was not cruelty. It was tidiness. The public slept soundly because someone kept the lie tidy, and she was that someone. Her lid did not save Gin. It did not save the twelve. It only made sure that whatever happened to them happened where nobody would have to look at it. Rei crossed it out before he had finished reading it. Crossing it out felt like the only easy decision of the month.
That left the three words, the kettle and the dark outside.
Rei sat in the cold kitchen with three words written under one sentence, and at last he saw the whole design of the trap. The trap was not any one of the words. The trap was that all three were true.

The Healer had not built a lie. It had built a true situation, where every honest way out cost Rei the very thing he had come to save. Then it had stood his loving brother in the middle of it, so that Rei could not walk away. Then it had waited. It had forty years behind it, and Rei had a month. An empty chair was always going to win a waiting game against a man who has to sleep.

He understood the registry now, completely, the way a man understands a sentence he would give his hands to unwrite. Twelve people held up the city by agreeing every morning to be crushed. One chair had stood open since the year the lights went grey. And the only people in Tokyo in a position to close it were two brothers the empty chair had spent six years quietly reaching for. One of them was already inside its reach. The other was sitting at a kitchen table at dawn, copying the wound into a notebook in his own rough handwriting.
Against every instinct he had left, he began to wonder whether love was the thing that would make him refuse the chair, or the thing that would put him in it.

Somewhere beyond the rooftops the first trains began to rumble, and a crow started up on the roof. The sky over the shrine roof turned from black to the colour of weak tea. There was one night left before the wall went double over the river, and one night after that before the festival ended. Rei pulled Gin's book back across the table and turned to the chapter he had skimmed and never read properly, the one with the drawings in it. Whatever he chose, he was going to need his brother's hands. The only place left to find them was on paper.
